paras: The lynching of C. D. Owens took place in Tampa, Florida, on March 6, 1882, when a mob took Owens, a young white man from London, from the jail and hanged him from a shade tree in front of the court house. Owens had been jailed about an hour earlier, accused of breaking into a house and attacking a young woman with a knife. Papers stressed that it happened in daylight beside the federal court, and Judge Locke later disbarred a Tampa attorney, Gen. Joseph B. Wall, for aiding it.

According to a Jacksonville Times correspondent, Owens was about thirty, had come from London about a year before, and made a poor living at odd jobs. On the night of Sunday, March 5, an intruder robbed the Nebraska Avenue home of a prominent citizen and entered his daughter's room. The correspondent and the Savannah Morning News said the intruder attempted rape and stabbed her several times with a bowie knife, leaving her "almost dying."

A posse captured Owens beyond Krause's Spring around noon the next day. By the correspondent's account, Owens admitted being in the house but said he meant only to rob it, and later spoke of rape; a signed dispatch from Tampa said he "made a confession of his guilt."

Owens was jailed at about one o'clock, and within an hour an "immense crowd" had gathered and voted to hang him. About twenty men seized the jail keys from Sheriff Craft at his dinner, took Owens out, and hurried him across the street to a large shade tree.

At the tree Owens denied the crime and asked for a trial, and someone in the crowd answered, "we will hang you first and try you afterwards." The sheriff and the mayor begged for his life, while Lieutenant Danes of the Third Artillery called the garrison to arms to rescue him. With his hands and feet tied, Owens was put on a dray under the tree; when the dray moved off the rope slipped, and half a dozen men pulled him up by the rope. The troops did not arrive in time, and the body hung in the street in front of the court house until sunset.

No report of an inquest or of arrests of the lynchers was found in the coverage. At the spring term of the federal court in Tampa, Judge Locke issued a rule against Gen. J. B. Wall to show cause why he should not be struck from the roll of attorneys "for counselling and aiding" the hanging, and then disbarred him. The Tampa Tribune complained that Locke acted on hearsay without a sworn complaint.

A Tampa correspondent of the Jacksonville Union, T. K. Spencer, reported "much feeling against Judge Locke" and called the disbarment political. In early April Wall applied to the U.S. Supreme Court for a mandamus to compel Locke to vacate the suspension.

Florida coverage began with a short dispatch to the Jacksonville Times, signed John P. Wall, which said Owens was hanged "by an outraged community." The Times correspondent's longer account, reprinted in the Tallahassee Floridian and in part in the Savannah Morning News, called Owens a "scoundrel" and "wretch" yet described the hanging as "one of the most awful tragedies" he had seen. Savannah's headline, "A Brute Hanged in Front of the Court House," took the accusation as proven.

A Pensacola wire dated March 18 ran on March 19 and 20 in St. Paul, Memphis, Salt Lake City and Wilmington under headlines such as "Murderer Lynched" and "Judge Lynch." Shortened digests carried it into Texas, Wisconsin and Alabama papers through March 25, stressing that the hanging took place "in full view of the United States court."

The wire's date of March 18, or "Saturday," conflicts with the Tampa dispatch dated March 6, Savannah's "Monday last" of March 14, and the Tampa Tribune's "6th inst."; the local sources are the better evidence. The Times correspondent and the wire said the federal court was in session, but Spencer wrote that "Court was not in session at the time of the affair"; the wire also put the tree in the court house yard rather than across the street.

A Tampa dispatch and a Times eyewitness correspondent (A1, A2), the Tampa Tribune (A22) and a separate Pensacola wire (A4, A5) agree that a mob took Owens from the Tampa jail and hanged him.

accounts.label: Tampa dispatch (John P. Wall)
accounts.gist: A tramp named Charles Owens was hanged in a Tampa street by 'an outraged community' for burglary and assault with intent to rape, after confessing.

accounts.label: Jacksonville Times correspondent (eyewitness)
accounts.gist: Owens was taken from jail while the federal court sat nearby and hanged across from the court house after a crowd vote; at the tree he denied the crime and begged for a trial, as the sheriff, mayor and an army officer tried to save him.

accounts.label: Pensacola wire
accounts.gist: Dated March 18, it says Owens stabbed a young lady 'today' and was taken from jail within an hour and hanged in the court house yard while the U.S. court was in session.

accounts.label: T. K. Spencer to the Jacksonville Union
accounts.gist: Court was not in session; Judge Locke struck Gen. Wall from the roll on witnesses' testimony, a step Spencer called political.

accounts.label: Tampa Tribune
accounts.gist: Judge Locke disbarred Wall on hearsay for aiding the hanging of March 6 without a sworn complaint, and the marshal's testimony did not bear out the rule.

framing.detail: The signed Tampa dispatch called the hangmen 'an outraged community' and said Owens confessed before 'meeting his fate'.

The Times correspondent called Owens a 'scoundrel' and 'miserable wretch' but described the hanging as 'one of the most awful tragedies' and closed asking God for more mercy than his fellow men showed.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'A Brute Hanged in Front of the Court House' and stated as fact that Owens acknowledged his guilt.
Wire copy ran under 'Murderer Lynched', 'A Terrible Crime and Swift Retribution' and 'Judge Lynch', presenting the stabbing as fact.
The Tampa Tribune called it 'the unlawful hanging of a man' but attacked Judge Locke's disbarment of Wall as arbitrary.
